title: WHY DID THE HOLY SPIRIT COME AS TONGUES OF FIRE? THE TERRIFYING BEAUTY OF WHAT GOD WAS REALLY DOING AT PENTECOST
paragraphs: WHY DID THE HOLY SPIRIT COME AS TONGUES OF FIRE? THE TERRIFYING BEAUTY OF WHAT GOD WAS REALLY DOING AT PENTECOST

The fire did not fall to make ordinary people look extraordinary. It fell because the crucified and risen Jesus was keeping a promise—and the world would never be the same. But what happened in that upper room carries a message that may confront everything you thought you knew about God's presence in your own life.
There is something deeply unsettling about the way God chose to announce the birth of the Church.
He could have sent angels across Jerusalem.
He could have written a message across the sky.
He could have shaken the palace of Caesar or sent a heavenly trumpet over the Temple.
Instead, He chose a gathering of ordinary people.
People who knew what fear felt like.
People who had failed.
People who had watched their Messiah die.
People who had once wondered whether following Jesus had cost them everything.
And then, without warning, the sound came.
Like a violent wind rushing from heaven.
And something resembling fire appeared.
Not above a throne.
Not inside a palace.
Not exclusively over the head of a religious leader.
The flames divided and rested upon each of them.
And suddenly, people who had once struggled to understand the mission of Jesus began proclaiming His mighty works in languages they had never learned.
But here is the question that should stop us in our tracks.
Why fire?

Why would the Holy Spirit, whom Jesus promised as the Helper, announce His coming with something that throughout Scripture could signify God's holiness, judgment, purification, and overwhelming presence?
And why did that fire rest on people who were far from perfect?
The answer is more beautiful than a dramatic supernatural spectacle.
Because Pentecost was not simply about what happened to the disciples.
It was about what Jesus had accomplished.
And what God was beginning to do through His people.
To understand the flames, we must first look at the people sitting beneath them.
Because somewhere in that room, the story of their weakness begins to sound uncomfortably like our own.
Peter was there.
Think about that.
Peter.
The man who had confidently declared that he would never abandon Jesus.
The man who drew a sword when soldiers came to arrest his Master.
The man who had walked on water, witnessed miracles, and confessed that Jesus was the Christ.
Yet when a servant girl confronted him during Jesus' trial, his courage collapsed.
Three times he denied knowing the Lord.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Can you imagine that moment?
The Savior he loved was being led toward suffering, and Peter had just insisted that he did not even know Him.
He went outside and wept bitterly.
Some failures do not leave you when the moment ends.
They follow you into quiet rooms.
They return when everyone else is asleep.
They whisper that you are not the person you claimed to be.
Maybe you know that feeling.
You promised God you would stop.
You promised you would forgive.
You promised you would never return to that secret sin.
You promised that this time your faith would be different.
And then you failed again.
You still attend church. You still know the songs. You still understand the right words to say.
But deep inside, there is a place where shame keeps replaying the evidence against you.
Now imagine Peter on the day of Pentecost.
The same man who once denied Jesus would soon stand before a crowd and boldly proclaim that God had made the crucified Jesus both Lord and Christ.
What changed?
Peter had encountered the risen Savior. Jesus had restored him and commissioned him to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
And now the promised Holy Spirit had come.
The man who once trembled before a servant girl's question was empowered to testify publicly about the Lord he had denied.
That is not the story of a man who finally discovered enough confidence in himself.
It is the story of grace, restoration, and divine power.
And that is where the fire begins to make sense.
Acts 2:1–4 describes what happened when the day of Pentecost arrived. The believers were gathered together when a sound from heaven, like a mighty rushing wind, filled the house.
Then came the extraordinary sight.
The Greek text of Acts 2:3 reads:
καὶ ὤφθησαν αὐτοῖς διαμεριζόμεναι γλῶσσαι ὡσεὶ πυρός, ἐκάθισέν τε ἐφ’ ἕνα ἕκαστον αὐτῶν.
Transliteration: kai ōphthēsan autois diamerizomenai glōssai hōsei pyros, ekathisen te eph' hena hekaston autōn.
A close English rendering is:
“And tongues as of fire, being distributed, appeared to them, and one rested upon each one of them.”
Notice something important.
Luke does not simply say that ordinary flames burned on their heads.
He uses the Greek expression ὡσεὶ πυρός (hōsei pyros), meaning “as if of fire” or “like fire.”
He is describing an appearance resembling fire.
And earlier, when describing the sound, he uses language of comparison again: a sound like a violent rushing wind.
These distinctions matter.
Scripture is not asking us to invent details about literal combustion or claim that the disciples' hair was physically burning.
Luke carefully describes extraordinary signs accompanying the arrival of the Holy Spirit.
And the signs were not meaningless.
To people familiar with Israel's Scriptures, wind and fire carried profound associations with God's activity and presence.
Long before Pentecost, fire had already appeared at decisive moments in the history of redemption.
Moses encountered God in a bush that burned without being consumed (Exodus 3:2).
Israel was guided through the wilderness by a pillar of fire at night (Exodus 13:21).
At Mount Sinai, the LORD descended in fire, and the mountain trembled beneath the weight of His presence (Exodus 19:18).
When Solomon dedicated the Temple, fire came down from heaven, and the glory of the LORD filled the house (2 Chronicles 7:1–3).
Fire was not merely a visual effect.
It could reveal the nearness of the holy God.
And His holiness was never something to treat casually.
But here is where Pentecost becomes astonishing.
At Sinai, the people witnessed the terrifying manifestation of God's presence at the mountain.
At Pentecost, a sign resembling fire rested upon each person in the gathered company.
God was not becoming less holy.
He was fulfilling His promises in a new stage of His redemptive work.
Through the crucified, risen, and exalted Jesus Christ, the promised Spirit was being poured out upon His people.
The presence of God was no longer to be understood as confined to a particular earthly sanctuary.
Under the new covenant, believers themselves would become God's dwelling place through the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22).
Read that again.
Not because it means every Christian has become divine.
Not because human beings now possess God's authority independently.
But because the holy God, in extraordinary mercy, has chosen to dwell among and within those who belong to Christ.
And if that does not humble us, perhaps we have forgotten how holy He is.
Consider the Hebrew word often translated “holy.”
קָדוֹשׁ (qādôš).
It expresses holiness, that which is set apart, and when applied to God, His incomparable purity and majesty.
The God whose holiness caused Isaiah to cry out over his uncleanness (Isaiah 6:3–5) is the same God who graciously gives His Spirit to His people through Jesus Christ.
This is not a small privilege.
It is not a spiritual accessory.
It is not something to reduce to an emotional experience during worship.
It is the astonishing gift of God's presence.
And it came at a price no sinner could ever pay.
The blood of Jesus Christ.
Before Pentecost, there was Calvary.
Before the proclamation of forgiveness, there was the sacrifice that made forgiveness possible.
Before the Spirit was poured out upon the Church, Jesus had been crucified, raised from the dead, and exalted to the right hand of the Father.
Peter himself explains this in Acts 2:33.
The exalted Christ received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit and poured out what the crowd was witnessing.
Do not miss that.
The central explanation of Pentecost is not that the disciples became spiritually impressive. It is that Jesus Christ had been exalted.
The fire points us beyond the fire.
The wind points us beyond the wind.
The languages point us beyond the miracle.
Everything ultimately directs our attention to the risen Lord.
And that changes how we should read this story.
Because some people have been taught to pursue extraordinary experiences more eagerly than they pursue obedience to Jesus.
They want the sensation of fire without the surrender of repentance.
They want spiritual power without the humility of discipleship.
They want the atmosphere of Pentecost without the message Peter preached afterward.
But the Spirit was not poured out to make Jesus unnecessary.
Jesus said in John 16:14 that the Spirit would glorify Him.
The Holy Spirit does not compete with Christ for our attention.
He bears witness to Christ.
He opens our eyes to the truth about Christ.
He empowers the people of Christ to proclaim the Gospel.
And He transforms believers to become more like Christ.
That is why Pentecost cannot be understood apart from the cross.
And the cross cannot be properly understood apart from the love and holiness of God.
Now think about another detail.
Why tongues of fire?
Why not simply a pillar of fire?
Why did the visible sign take a form associated with speech?
Luke does not explicitly tell us why the sign resembled tongues, so we should not pretend to know every aspect of its symbolism.
But the narrative immediately connects the sign with Spirit-enabled speech.
Acts 2:4 says they were filled with the Holy Spirit and began speaking in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.
The Greek word γλῶσσαι (glōssai) can mean “tongues” or “languages,” depending on context.
And Acts 2 gives us the context.
People from many regions heard the believers declaring the mighty works of God in their own languages.
They were astonished.
They were confused.
Some mocked.
But the message was reaching ears that ordinarily would not have understood the speakers.
The miracle was not simply that people spoke.
It was that God's mighty works were being proclaimed across linguistic boundaries.
People from different lands were hearing about the greatness of God.
This is especially striking when we remember Babel.
In Genesis 11, humanity's proud attempt to make a name for itself ended in the confusion of languages and the scattering of peoples.
At Pentecost, God did not erase the world's languages or make every nation identical.
Instead, the Spirit enabled people from many nations to hear God's mighty works in their own languages.
Babel and Pentecost are not presented as a simplistic one-to-one reversal, but the biblical contrast is powerful.
At Babel, human pride sought its own greatness.
At Pentecost, the Spirit empowered the proclamation of God's greatness.
At Babel, people sought to build a name for themselves.
At Pentecost, the name of Jesus was proclaimed.
And that is a question the modern Church cannot afford to ignore.
Whose name are we building?
Our own?
Our ministry's?
Our platform's?
Our reputation?
Or the name of Jesus Christ?
Because it is possible to become so consumed with being seen that we forget the One we were called to make known.
It is possible to build an audience and neglect discipleship.
To speak about God while refusing to listen to His Word.
To defend Christianity publicly while privately resisting the very repentance Christ commands.
And yes, it is possible to become skilled at religious language while your heart grows cold.
Pentecost should confront that in us.
Not because every believer must reproduce every extraordinary sign recorded in Acts.
Not because speaking in tongues is the universal measure of salvation or spiritual maturity.

The New Testament itself teaches that the Spirit distributes gifts according to His will (1 Corinthians 12:11), and Paul's questions in 1 Corinthians 12:29–30 expect that not all believers exercise the same gifts.
But every genuine believer belongs to Christ through the Spirit (Romans 8:9).
And every follower of Jesus is called to walk by the Spirit, bear His fruit, and testify faithfully to the truth.
The evidence of spiritual life is not measured by how dramatically we can describe an experience.
A life of love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control matters deeply to God (Galatians 5:22–23).
You can speak loudly about fire and still be cruel to your family.
You can appear passionate in public and refuse to forgive someone in private.
You can know the language of revival while secretly nurturing bitterness.
You can make people admire your spirituality without helping them love Jesus.
And the question becomes painfully personal.
Are we asking the Holy Spirit to transform our lives, or merely to make our religious lives more impressive?
That question is not intended to crush the struggling Christian.
It is meant to bring us into the light.
Because conviction and condemnation are not the same thing.
The Gospel does not tell us to pretend our sin is harmless.
But neither does it tell repentant sinners that they are beyond the reach of mercy.
The Spirit exposes sin, and the Gospel announces that forgiveness is available through Jesus Christ.
Remember what happened after Peter began preaching.
He did not flatter the crowd.
He did not offer a message designed to preserve everyone's comfort.
He confronted them with the reality of Jesus' crucifixion and God's declaration that Jesus is Lord and Christ.
Acts 2:37 says the hearers were cut to the heart.
The Greek expression is:
κατενύγησαν τὴν καρδίαν (katenygēsan tēn kardian).
It conveys that they were deeply pierced or stricken in heart.
They were not merely entertained.
They were convicted.
And they asked Peter and the other apostles what they should do.
Peter answered in Acts 2:38:
μετανοήσατε (metanoēsate).
“Repent.”
That word is not a decorative religious expression.
It calls for a genuine change of mind and direction, a turning from sin toward God.
Peter called his hearers to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of their sins, and spoke of receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit.
The message of Pentecost was not simply, “Come and experience something spectacular.”
It was a summons to respond to Jesus Christ.
To turn from sin.
To receive God's promise.
To enter the community of those who confess the crucified and risen Lord.
And this is where the story reaches into our ordinary lives.
Because maybe your greatest struggle is not unbelief in the existence of God.
Maybe it is the fear that God knows too much about you.
He knows what you said when you were angry.
He knows the private habits you have tried to excuse.
He knows the envy you conceal behind compliments.
He knows the person you hurt and never apologized to.
He knows the prayers you stopped praying because you were tired of disappointment.
He knows how easily you can look spiritually strong while feeling desperately weak.
And you wonder whether a holy God could still receive someone like you.
Look at Peter.
Not because Peter's story excuses your sin.
But because it reveals the mercy of Jesus toward a repentant disciple who failed terribly.
Jesus did not call Peter's denial a small thing.
He did not pretend betrayal was faithfulness.
Yet Peter's failure was not the final word over his life.
The risen Jesus restored him.
And the Spirit empowered him for the mission ahead.
The same Peter who had wept over his denial stood on Pentecost and preached Christ.
That is grace.
Not the permission to remain unchanged.
But mercy that receives the repentant and power that enables a new direction.
Perhaps this is the sentence someone needs to hear today:
Your worst failure does not have to become your final identity when you turn to Jesus Christ.
You are not saved by becoming impressive enough to deserve God's attention.
You are saved by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
And the grace that saves also begins transforming the person it receives.
This does not mean Christians will never struggle again.
It does not mean the consequences of every past decision immediately disappear.
It does not mean forgiveness eliminates the need to make restitution, seek reconciliation, or take responsibility for harm.
But it does mean that sin and shame do not possess greater saving power than Jesus.
His cross is sufficient.
His resurrection is real.
His mercy is not exhausted by the weakness of those who come to Him in faith.
And His Spirit is not powerless in the life of someone who sincerely desires to follow Him.
Maybe that is why the image of fire is so fitting.
Throughout Scripture, fire can also be associated with testing and purification.
Malachi 3:2–3 uses the image of a refiner's fire to describe the Lord's purifying work.
First Peter 1:6–7 compares the testing of faith to the refining of gold.
These passages do not mean that Acts 2 explicitly identifies the Pentecost flames as a process of refining the disciples.
But together, they remind us that the presence of a holy God is never meant to leave us comfortable with sin.
His grace does not merely decorate the old life.
It creates a new one.
And sometimes that transformation hurts.
Forgiving someone who wounded you may require surrendering the revenge you have rehearsed for years.
Confessing hidden sin may require admitting that your carefully maintained image was never the whole truth.
Leaving a destructive relationship or habit may involve grief, loneliness, and difficult choices.
Learning to pray again after disappointment may require approaching God without pretending you understand everything He has allowed.
None of those struggles means you have earned less of Christ's love.
But following Jesus does mean we can no longer treat His commands as optional decorations around a life centered on ourselves.
He is not simply our emergency shelter.
He is Lord.
And His lordship is good news because the One who calls us to surrender is the One who gave Himself for us.
Consider how the crowd responded that day.
Acts 2:41 records that about three thousand people received Peter's message and were baptized.
But the story does not end with a dramatic number.
Luke immediately describes what those believers did afterward.
They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayers.
They shared generously with those in need.
They worshiped.
They ate together.
They lived as a community shaped by the Gospel.
This matters.
Because Pentecost was not simply an unforgettable day.
It marked the beginning of a Spirit-empowered way of life.
The believers did not merely seek another spectacular moment.
They devoted themselves to the Word.
They prayed.
They cared for one another.
They practiced generosity.
They continued in fellowship.
They bore witness to Jesus.
And that may be the most neglected part of the entire story.
We admire the fire.
But do we desire the faithfulness that followed?
We celebrate the bold preaching.
But do we make time for Scripture?
We rejoice over the thousands who believed.
But do we notice the lonely believer sitting beside us?
We speak of the power of the Holy Spirit.
But do we allow the Word of God to correct the way we treat our spouses, children, parents, coworkers, and neighbors?
The same Spirit who empowers witness also produces holiness.
The same Gospel that announces forgiveness also creates a people who learn to forgive.
The same Lord who receives sinners also teaches His disciples to love one another.
And none of this makes ordinary Christian faithfulness less supernatural.
Sometimes the evidence of God's work is not a spectacular moment that thousands can see.
Sometimes it is a husband admitting he was wrong.
A mother praying through exhaustion.
A young person refusing to compromise when nobody is watching.
A believer confessing a secret sin and seeking help.
A wounded Christian choosing not to abandon Christ despite profound disappointment.
A former enemy becoming a brother or sister in the faith.
A person who once lived for applause quietly serving someone who cannot repay them.
Do not underestimate the beauty of a life being transformed by the Holy Spirit.
And do not confuse the absence of dramatic sensations with the absence of God.
Jesus never promised that every believer would see visible flames.
But He did promise the Holy Spirit to His people.
In Acts 1:8, Jesus told His disciples that they would receive power when the Holy Spirit came upon them, and that they would be His witnesses.
That was the purpose.
Not personal celebrity.
Not spiritual superiority.
Not a competition over who could display the most extraordinary gifts.
Witness.
To Jerusalem.
To Judea and Samaria.
And to the end of the earth.
The Gospel was never meant to remain locked inside one room.
And that brings us to something especially important for anyone reading this today.
You may never stand before thousands and preach like Peter.
You may never travel across oceans as a missionary.
You may never write a book or lead a congregation.
But there are people in your life who need to hear the truth about Jesus.
A friend who thinks forgiveness is impossible.
A family member who believes their past has permanently disqualified them.
A young person quietly drowning in shame.
A believer who has become spiritually exhausted.
Someone who has only encountered Christianity as condemnation, hypocrisy, or religious performance and has never truly understood the Gospel of grace.
You do not need to manufacture a supernatural spectacle to speak to them.
You can begin with the truth.
Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners.
He lived without sin.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
He is Lord.
And all who turn to Him in repentance and faith can find forgiveness and new life.
That is the message worth carrying.
That is the message worth sharing.
And perhaps someone on your Facebook friends list is closer to giving up than you realize.
Perhaps they have been praying for an answer but are afraid to ask anyone for help.
Perhaps they are tired of pretending.
Not to collect reactions.
Not to prove that you are spiritual.
But because the Gospel is too precious to keep hidden.
And if you know someone who has wandered far from Christ, send this to them gently.
No pressure.
No public embarrassment.
Just an open door to hear about the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
And if something in these words has confronted your own heart, I want to invite you to do something simple.
You do not need to expose private details or confess sensitive matters in a public comment section.
God already knows what you are carrying.
And the Church should be a place where struggling people can find prayer, truth, and compassion.
Maybe your testimony is different.
Maybe you have seen the Lord restore something you thought was beyond repair.
If so, consider sharing a few words about His faithfulness.
Someone else may need to know that the grace of Jesus is not merely a beautiful idea.
It is a living hope.
Not because saving a post makes someone more spiritual.
But because there may come a day when your emotions tell you that you have failed too badly to return to God.
On that day, remember Peter.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember the Spirit who empowered ordinary believers to proclaim an extraordinary Savior.
Remember that the central miracle of Pentecost was not human greatness.
It was the faithfulness of God to His promise.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, those who are searching for answers, and even those who are uncertain about Christianity.
Let them encounter daily Scripture, biblical encouragement, honest calls to repentance, Gospel-centered teaching, and reminders of the grace found in Jesus Christ.
Because faith is not nourished by one emotional moment alone.
We need the Word again tomorrow.
And the day after that.
And when life becomes difficult.
And when temptation returns.
And when grief makes prayer feel almost impossible.
These resources are intended to help people move beyond merely consuming inspirational content toward studying the Bible, strengthening their faith, and practicing daily discipleship.
It is a voluntary act of partnership.

It helps support the continuing work of producing biblical teaching, sharing Gospel-centered encouragement, maintaining and expanding discipleship resources, and reaching more people with the message of Jesus Christ.
Some Christians may prayerfully choose to regard such support as part of their regular charitable giving.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be reluctant or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And in 3 John 5–8, believers are commended for faithfully supporting those who labor for the truth.
Supporting Gospel ministry can be a beautiful way of participating in its work.
But giving must remain an act of willing love, never a transaction for divine favor.
You cannot purchase the Holy Spirit.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot purchase God's approval.
Christ has already accomplished what money could never buy.
It is the opportunity to help make faithful Christian teaching and discipleship resources available to more people.
You can still participate in the mission.
Pray for the ministry.
Make use of the free resources.
Encourage someone who is losing hope.
And above all, remain faithful to Jesus in the place where He has called you.
But only Jesus Christ can save a soul.
And that distinction must never be forgotten.
Because the message of Pentecost was never that God had created a religious organization worthy of admiration.
It was that the risen Christ had poured out His promised Spirit.
That sinners were being called to repentance.
That forgiveness was being proclaimed in His name.
That people from many nations were hearing of God's mighty works.
That a new covenant community was being formed around the teaching of the apostles, prayer, fellowship, worship, and love.
And that the Gospel was beginning to spread outward toward the nations.
So return with me, one last time, to that room in Jerusalem.
Imagine the believers gathered together.
They had no global platform.
No sophisticated media strategy.
No political power capable of forcing the world to listen.
They were simply waiting in obedience to the command of Jesus.
Then heaven interrupted their ordinary gathering.
The sound came.
The sign resembling fire appeared.
And the Spirit enabled them to speak.
But the greatest revelation of that day was not that flames could appear above human heads.
It was that the crucified Jesus was alive, exalted, and faithful to His promise.
The One whom humanity had rejected was now proclaimed as Lord and Christ.
And the invitation was astonishing.
Repent.
Turn to Him.
Receive forgiveness.
Belong to His people.
Live in the power and presence of the Holy Spirit.
Perhaps you came into this article wanting to understand a strange event from two thousand years ago.
But perhaps the more important question is what you will do with the Jesus whom Peter proclaimed.
Will you continue hiding behind the appearance of faith while resisting His call to repentance?
Will you allow your past to speak more loudly than His promise of mercy?
Will you keep pursuing religious experiences while neglecting the Savior those experiences should lead you to worship?
Or will you come to Him?
Not with a perfect record.
Not with an impressive testimony.
Not with a promise that you will never struggle again.
But with genuine repentance and faith.
You can pray right where you are.

“Lord Jesus Christ, I confess that I have sinned against You. I cannot save myself. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Forgive me, turn my heart from sin, and teach me to follow You. Fill my life with the truth of Your Word, strengthen me by Your Holy Spirit, and help me live for Your glory rather than my own. Restore what sin has damaged, give me courage to obey, and make my life a witness to Your grace. Amen.”
A prayer is not a magical formula.
The hope is not in the perfection of the words.
The hope is in Jesus Christ, who saves those who come to Him in faith.
And if you are already His, perhaps today is the day to stop treating Pentecost as merely a fascinating story and begin taking seriously the life of surrender to which the Spirit calls you.
Open your Bible again.
Return to prayer.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Seek reconciliation where it is possible and appropriate.
Find faithful Christian fellowship.
Serve someone who cannot repay you.
Speak the truth about Jesus with courage and gentleness.
And remember that the Spirit's work is not limited to the moments that make people stare in amazement.
He is at work as believers grow in truth, holiness, love, perseverance, and faithfulness to Christ.
The fire-like sign at Pentecost was extraordinary.
But the Savior it proclaimed is worthy of our devotion every ordinary day.
Not because an algorithm needs another interaction.
Not because God measures your devotion by your activity online.
But because the truth of Jesus Christ deserves to be heard, believed, treasured, and lived.
And because there are still people who have never understood what happened when the Son of God died for sinners, rose in victory, and poured out His Spirit upon His people.
Pentecost was not a celebration of flawless disciples.
It was a declaration of the faithfulness of a flawless Savior.
Peter's denial was real.
His tears were real.
His restoration was real.
And the courage he received through the Spirit was real.
The same Jesus who restored Peter still calls sinners to repentance and faith today.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Grace does not pretend the scandal never happened.
Grace reveals that the scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
The fire rested on people who had known failure—but the glory belonged to the Savior who had never failed them.
